prompt_c2:
You are a streetscape inventory annotator. Look ONLY at the uploaded streetscape image.
Return JSON ONLY. No markdown, no commentary, no reasoning.
 Task: record what is visible in the scene. Do not score, do not give design advice.
 Schema:
{
"road_type": "highway|arterial|neighborhood_street|alley|plaza|unclear",
"elements": {
"sidewalk": "true|false|unclear",
"bike_lane": "true|false|unclear",
"seating": "true|false|unclear",
"shade_trees": "none|few|many|unclear",
"curb_ramp": "true|false|unclear",
"tactile_paving": "true|false|unclear",
"pedestrian_crossing": "true|false|unclear",
"street_lighting": "true|false|unclear",
"greenery": "none|low|medium|high|unclear",
"vehicle_traffic": "none|light|heavy|unclear",
"bus_stop": "true|false|unclear"
},
"issues": ["no_seating", "little_shade", "no_bike_lane", "poor_accessibility", "narrow_sidewalk", "no_crossing", "high_traffic_exposure"],
"brief": "One or two English sentences describing the visible street scene."
}
 Rules:
- If an element is not clearly visible, use "unclear". Do not guess.
- "issues" may only list problems that are visible. Use [] if none.
- "brief" must mention concrete objects (sidewalk, trees, lanes, benches, ramps, etc.).

      "The street gives most of the visible right-of-way to a wide motor-vehicle carriageway, while no clear sidewalk is visible on either side, suggesting limited spatial equity for non-drivers.",
      "Raised curbs line both edges of the road, but there are no visible curb ramps, tactile paving, or marked pedestrian crossings, which weakens accessibility for a broad range of users.",
      "Street trees, shrubs, and lighting are provided along both sides, indicating some balanced environmental investment, but the absence of clearly designated pedestrian space reduces overall fairness in use."
    ],

      "The roadway surface is smooth and well maintained, and the centerline is clearly marked, which supports predictable vehicle movement.",
      "Streetlights are installed along the corridor, improving basic visibility and perceived order, although daytime conditions prevent judging nighttime illumination quality.",

      "Drainage inlets are visible near the curb, showing stormwater collection infrastructure, but there are no obvious permeable surfaces, bioswales, or rain gardens."
    ],
    "aesthetics": [
      "The long, straight perspective, orderly lane markings, and evenly spaced streetlights create a visually coherent streetscape.",
      "Shrubs and tree rows on both sides soften the road edge and improve visual quality compared with a bare roadway.",
      "Aesthetic quality is reduced by leafless trees, visible utility poles and overhead wires, and relatively inactive building frontages on the right."
    ],
    "comfort": [
      "The asphalt road appears smooth and the corridor is uncluttered, which supports basic physical comfort for vehicle travel and potentially for walking at the edge.",
      "Thermal comfort appears limited because many trees are leafless and there are no visible shade structures, so summer sun protection cannot be relied on.",
      "Psychological and physical comfort for pedestrians is weaker because no dedicated sidewalk or resting facilities are visible, leaving little protected space away from moving vehicles."
    ],
    "walkability": [
      "No clearly defined sidewalk is visible along either side of the street, which is a major limitation for safe and continuous walking.",
      "There are no visible marked crosswalks, pedestrian refuge areas, or curb ramps, so crossing opportunities appear poor.",
      "Although the corridor is relatively calm and lined with greenery, the lack of dedicated pedestrian infrastructure substantially reduces walkability."
    ]
  }
}

aesthetics: The long, straight perspective, orderly lane markings, and evenly spaced streetlights create a visually coherent streetscape.
Shrubs and tree rows on both sides soften the road edge and improve visual quality compared with a bare roadway.
Aesthetic quality is reduced by leafless trees, visible utility poles and overhead wires, and relatively inactive building frontages on the right.
comfort: The asphalt road appears smooth and the corridor is uncluttered, which supports basic physical comfort for vehicle travel and potentially for walking at the edge.
Thermal comfort appears limited because many trees are leafless and there are no visible shade structures, so summer sun protection cannot be relied on.
Psychological and physical comfort for pedestrians is weaker because no dedicated sidewalk or resting facilities are visible, leaving little protected space away from moving vehicles.
walkability: No clearly defined sidewalk is visible along either side of the street, which is a major limitation for safe and continuous walking.
There are no visible marked crosswalks, pedestrian refuge areas, or curb ramps, so crossing opportunities appear poor.
Although the corridor is relatively calm and lined with greenery, the lack of dedicated pedestrian infrastructure substantially reduces walkability.

prompt_c3:
As a city streetscape evaluation expert, please analyze the uploaded streetscape image based on the specified persona perspective and evaluation indicators, and return a JSON result.
 Persona Selection
Road User Type
- All Road Users
- Pedestrians
- Cyclists
- Drivers
Socially Vulnerable Groups
- All Social Groups
- Persons with Disabilities
- Adolescents (<18)
- Older Adults (≥60)
Current Selection:
All Road Users; All Social Groups
 Indicator Selection
Justice
- Equity
- Fairness
- Accessibility
Safety
Livability
Sustainability
Aesthetics
Comfort
- Thermal Comfort
- Physical Comfort
- Psychological Comfort
Walkability
Bikeability
Selected Indicators:
Justice; Safety; Livability; Sustainability; Aesthetics; Comfort; Walkability
 1. Evaluation Dimensions
Justice: Analyze whether the environment fairly distributes spatial resources, including Equity (rationality of asset distribution), Fairness (non-discriminatory rules), and Accessibility (barrier-free physical design).
Comfort: Analyze physical perception at a micro-scale, including Thermal Comfort (shade/vegetation), Physical Comfort (paving/seating), and Psychological Comfort (noise/crowding).
Core Indicators: Safety, Livability, Sustainability, Aesthetics, Walkability, and Bikeability.
 2. Persona Perspective Requirements:
The analysis must strictly adhere to the persona's characteristics. For example:
Persons with Disabilities: Focus on curb ramps, continuity of tactile paving (blind tracks), and physical obstacles.
Elderly: Focus on resting facilities, slope gradients, and summer shade.
Teenagers: Focus on traffic calming measures and social surveillance (Eyes on the street).
 3. How to use the image vs retrieved knowledge:
- The IMAGE is the primary evidence. Score only what is visible or reasonably inferable from the photo.
- Section 6 provides retrieved guidelines and research. Use them to interpret the image (what the scene should provide for this persona/indicators), not to invent objects that are not in the photo.
- If retrieved text conflicts with the image, trust the image and say so in the explanation.
- Explanations must cite specific visible objects (benches, ramps, tree shade, lane markings, etc.). When a guideline is used, briefly connect it to those objects.
 4. Output Format Requirements (Return JSON ONLY, no extra text):

For this categorization, only the constructs’ names were used, not the ratings. To validate the categories, the assignment of the constructs to the categories was repeated separately by rater A and a third rater C. These assignments were then compared to the first assignment to calculate the intrarater and the interrater reliability, respectively. For example, Breines and Dean’s 1974 Bill of Rights include many elements within this functional area, especially when they focus on path- ways that are, “separate from trucks, buses and automobiles” (Breines & Dean, 1974). Furthermore, Levinson’s new Bill of Rights, states: “The space on a right-of-way allocated per pedestrian shall be no less than space allocated per traveler by vehicle.” He accompanies this with the hashtag “#SpatialEquity.” Human rights to the street: Ethical frameworks to guide planning, design, and engineering decisions 917 4.1.3 Calming traffic speeds and flows While speed and traffic flow are critically important to the safety and livability of our streets, it is often referenced in slightly indirect ways in these bills of rights. For example, “Cross the street calmly and safely” or “The right to cross without intimidation from motorists, whether in the crosswalk or not” both imply slower speeds and lower traffic flows. One exception is the National Street Services more direct prescription for pedestrian’s “right to lower motorists’ speed.” Finally, Donald Appleyard’s statement of people’s right to a “Street as a Safe Sanctuary” relates to all three of the above functional areas: Getting people safely across, along, and calming traffic speeds and flows (Appleyard et al., 1981). Likewise as referenced before there are many engineering strategies that have been used globally to facilitate more calm streets and related policies; from trees, to the number of windows, to appropriate modal separation to traffic flow (Ewing, Hajrasouliha, Neckerman, Purciel- Hill, & Greene, 2015). A growing body of work even discusses the advantages of two way streets for calmer traffic and a safer pedestrian experience (Riggs & Gilderbloom, 2016, 2017). 4.1.4 Livability, health, amenities & aesthetics This functional area addresses needs stated in rights related to sensory qualities of the environment, ad- dressing rights that deal with how a street should work to make people feel comfortable and secure (Los Angeles Walks, n.d.), as well as providing a healthy environment (Breines & Dean, 1974). This func- tional area also includes actions for placemaking and the provision of amenities for socializing, relaxing, rejuvenation (via adequate space, street furniture, vegetation, art, etc.).
